learning_objective: 🎯 Trace the journey from colonial printing presses to 24/7 news channels, and see how media shapes public opinion and democracy!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: During colonial times, newspapers were a tool for nationalist leaders to unite the country. Today, India is unique because print media (especially regional language newspapers) is still growing rapidly.
Initially, All India Radio and Doordarshan were state-controlled and focused on education and nation-building. After 1991, satellite TV brought hundreds of private, profit-driven commercial channels.
The merging of Information and Entertainment. News channels increasingly use dramatic music, sensational headlines, and debate formats to grab ratings, rather than just delivering dry facts.
The internet and social media have changed communication from one-way (broadcasting) to two-way (interactive). Audiences are now also content creators.

fun_activity.title: 🗞️ Front Page Analysis
fun_activity.instructions: Pick up today's newspaper and a regional language newspaper. Count how many articles on the front page are about politics, how many are about entertainment, and how much space is given to advertisements. Compare the two!

exam_tips: 📌 A common question is 'Why is Print Media still growing in India despite the internet?' Answer: Rising literacy rates, local news coverage, and bundling supplements.
📌 Contrast the role of Doordarshan in the 1980s (social messaging like Hum Log) with modern private TV networks.
📌 Mention the impact of structural changes (liberalisation) on the media becoming a massive corporate industry.
quick_recap: ⭐ The first modern mass media institution in India was the printing press introduced by the British.
⭐ Transnational television companies localise their content to capture Indian audiences (e.g., Star TV adapting to Hindi programming).
⭐ Mass media acts as the 'watchdog' of a vibrant democracy.
